stages.title: First Session
stages.details:
Inaugural Meeting The Constituent Assembly met for the first time in New Delhi.

Objective Resolution Introduced by Jawaharlal Nehru on Dec 13, laying the philosophical fundamentals.

stages.title: Second Session
stages.details: Resolution Adopted The Assembly unanimously adopted the Objective Resolution on January 22, 1947.

stages.title: Third Session
stages.details: Princely States Join Representatives from the Princely States took their seats in the Assembly.

stages.title: Fourth Session
stages.details: National Flag On July 22, 1947, the Assembly adopted the Free India National Flag.

stages.title: Fifth Session
stages.details:
Midnight Session The Assembly met at midnight on August 14 to assume power for independent India.

Drafting Committee Appointed on August 29, 1947, with Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as its Chairman.

stages.title: Sixth Session
stages.details: Short Session A brief session held to discuss minor procedural matters.

stages.title: Seventh Session
stages.details: First Reading Dr. B.R. Ambedkar introduced the final Draft Constitution and delivered a brilliant speech defending its provisions.

stages.title: Eighth Session
stages.details: Debates Continue Intensive clause-by-clause debates continued, focusing heavily on Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

stages.title: Ninth Session
stages.details: Crucial Debates The Assembly saw fierce debates regarding the Official Language and Citizenship.

stages.title: Tenth Session
stages.details: Second Reading Completed The second reading of the Constitution, the most rigorous part of the drafting process, was finally concluded.

stages.title: Eleventh Session
stages.details:
Third Reading Final revisions and the third reading of the draft.

Adoption Day On November 26, 1949, the Constitution was officially adopted, enacted, and given to the people of India.

stages.title: Final Meeting
stages.details:
Signatures The Assembly met once again on 24 January, 1950, when the members appended their signatures to the Constitution of India.

National Anthem & Song 'Jana Gana Mana' and 'Vande Mataram' adopted.

committees.details:
Overview: Tasked with examining the initial working draft prepared by the Constitutional Advisor and structuring the comprehensive blueprint of the Indian Constitution.

Recognized as the primary architectural body in the making of the Republic, the Drafting Committee was entrusted with the monumental duty of creating the final text of the Constitution. Upon its formation in August 1947, the group was faced with the colossal challenge of synthesizing reports, recommendations, and decisions from all other functional sub-committees.

Their foundation was the comprehensive, albeit raw, structural draft prepared by Constitutional Advisor B.N. Rau. Under the visionary stewardship of Chairman Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the committee meticulously reviewed and revised this bedrock text line by line. The grueling process saw them balancing divergent philosophies regarding state power, fundamental rights, and executive autonomy.

In February 1948, the committee published the first Draft Constitution consisting of 315 articles and 8 schedules. It was then placed before the Indian public and provincial legislatures for intense scrutiny, accumulating over 7,000 proposed amendments over a period of eight months. The committee methodically debated thousands of these revisions before championing the final document through the Assembly's grueling reading phases.
committees.title: Drafting Committee

committees.details:
Overview: An overarching advisory body responsible for formulating robust safeguards for minority communities, tribal populations, and establishing the core justiciable rights of citizens.

The majestic Advisory Committee acted as the supreme umbrella organization charged with integrating the socio-political rights of India's massively diverse population. Because handling rights and minorities was an intensely complex and sensitive issue in a newly partitioned India, the Assembly mandated this singular powerhouse committee (with over 54 members) to coordinate these efforts across multiple sub-committees.

Under Sardar Patel's unifying leadership, the committee debated extensively on bridging extreme ideological divides. They tackled controversial issues ranging from religious freedom and reservations in the public sector, to language barriers and cultural preservation rights. The committee was fundamentally responsible for guaranteeing that the core tenets of the Constitution were undeniably secular and democratic.

Their final reports aggregated the findings of the sub-committees on Minorities, Fundamental Rights, and Tribal Excluded Areas. By advocating for universal adult franchise while simultaneously rejecting separate electorates (in favor of highly controlled safeguards), the committee established the egalitarian framework of modern independent India.
committees.title: Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights & Minorities

committees.details:
Overview: Deliberated on the extent of federal authority, defining the jurisdiction, responsibilities, and legislative powers of the Central Government over Union subjects.

The Union Powers Committee was organized with an intensely critical mandate: to decisively settle the distribution of power between the newly forming federal central government and its constituent provinces. In the volatile, tragic aftermath of the subcontinent’s partition, the committee's outlook fundamentally shifted from a loose federation toward advocating for a fiercely capable, centralized authority.

Recognizing that a weak center could lead to national disintegration and severe economic fracturing, Jawaharlal Nehru and his team strongly recommended retaining significant fiscal and administrative leverage at the Union level. They designated exclusive national authority over critical domains such as defense, foreign affairs, inter-state communications, and national currency.

Their meticulously analyzed reports formed the constitutional backbone of India's robust federal structure, introducing the Union List paradigm that ensures uniformity while still allowing provincial autonomy in concurrent areas.
committees.title: Union Powers Committee

committees.details:
Overview: Focused on the administrative and legislative frameworks for individual provinces iteratively, balancing regional autonomy with the necessity of national unity.

While the Union Powers Committee crafted the massive machinery of the central apparatus, the Provincial Constitution Committee architected the governance model for the states (which were then termed provinces). Sardar Patel, possessing immense experience and political acuity in integrating the diverse princely states, led the deliberations on how provincial executives, legislatures, and state relations should structurally operate.

A highly consequential debate within the committee centered around the role of the Governor. Some members advocated for adopting the American presidential model, pushing for an elected Governor with independent executive authority. Alternatively, others warned this would conflict directly with the Chief Minister and foster instability.

Ultimately, to maintain structural harmony across the nascent nation, they chose the British parliamentary model. They ensured that the Governor acted as a constitutional head functioning entirely on the binding advice of a council of ministers led by a democratically elected Chief Minister, thereby perfectly mirroring the federal layout at the state level.
committees.title: Provincial Constitution Committee

committees.details:
Overview and Objectives: The Committee on the Rules of Procedure was established to define the operational framework of the Constituent Assembly. Its mandate included drafting the regulations governing the Assembly's various segments and sub-committees, ensuring a standardized method of operation across the board.

Formation (December 10, 1946)
On December 10, 1946, J.B. Kripalani moved a resolution to appoint a committee consisting of a Chairman and 15 members to frame the Rules of Procedure. In his initial draft, Kripalani had removed the words "Sections and Committees," believing them to be superfluous, though he later accepted their inclusion following significant debate.

As per the final resolution, the committee was tasked with reporting on:

  • Rules of Procedure: For the Assembly, including its Sections and Committees.
  • Powers of the Chairman: Defining the authority of the presiding officer.
  • Organization of Work: Including the appointment, functions, and powers of office-bearers.
  • Vacancies: The procedure for the declaration and filling of vacancies.

The Debate on Jurisdiction and "Indivisibility"
A significant debate occurred regarding whether the Assembly should explicitly legislate for its "Sections."
Pro-clarity Stance: Dr. Suresh Chandra Banerjee and Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee insisted that the rules explicitly apply to "Sections and Committees" to prevent future ambiguity. Mookerjee argued that without this, sections might claim independent authority to frame their own rules. This was supported by Purushottam Das Tandon and Sarat Chandra Bose, who argued that clear wording would resolve conflicts in advance.
The Concept of "One and Indivisible": K.M. Munshi argued that omitting these words might imply the Assembly was not a self-determining institution. He emphasized that the Assembly was "one and indivisible" and that no section could function inconsistently with the general rules.
The Cautious Approach: M.R. Jayakar and S.H. Prater urged caution. Jayakar warned that explicitly mentioning sections might create suspicion or hostility among the "absent group" (the Muslim League), potentially hindering their future participation.
Sovereignty: Debi Prasad Khaitan countered the cautious view, stating the Assembly must proceed with its work for the whole country regardless of who was absent. Jawaharlal Nehru ultimately advised Kripalani to accept the amendment to include "Sections and Committees" to settle the misapprehension.

Minority Representation and the Role of Sardar Harnam Singh
One of the most critical aspects of the debate involved ensuring that smaller minority groups were not sidelined during the rulemaking process.
Sardar Harnam Singh's Advocacy: Singh played a pivotal role in refining the committee's structure and language. He specifically suggested the wording should be "its Sections and Committees" to emphasize the relationship between the Assembly and its sub-units.
Concerns for the Advisory Committee: Singh expressed significant concern regarding the Advisory Committee (intended to protect fundamental rights and minority interests). He feared that through proportional representation alone, minorities might not have a sufficient voice in framing the rules for such a sensitive body. To mitigate this, he proposed that 10 members be elected and 5 be nominated by the Chairman to ensure adequate minority representation.
The Co-option Amendment: When the idea of co-option was introduced by other members to add absent friends later, Sardar Harnam Singh successfully amended the proposal by adding a critical limit: the committee should have the power to co-opt "not more than five" members.

Final Decision on Co-option
Concern was raised by Sardar Harnam Singh and Sardar Ujjal Singh that proportional representation might leave smaller minorities without a seat. While J.B. Kripalani initially opposed co-option, the amendment—as refined by Singh’s five-member limit—was adopted to ensure a wider inclusive framework. This was supported by B.G. Kher and Jairamdas Daulatram.

Procedural and Technical Contributions
Several members contributed to the technical refinement of the committee's mandate:
H.V. Kamath: Successfully proposed adding the word "functions" to the clause concerning office-bearers and noted the need for a Tribunal to handle election petitions. His suggestion to change "filling of vacancies" to "filling in" was rejected following an objection by Diwan Chaman Lall.
Mohan Lal Saksena: Moved an amendment regarding the election process for the committee, ensuring that if nominations were fewer than vacancies, those nominated would be declared elected immediately.
H.J. Khandekar: Suggested using "he or she" to acknowledge lady members. The Chairman, Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, ruled that legally, "he" inherently includes "she."
R.V. Dhulekar and the Language Debate: Dhulekar moved an amendment that the Procedure Committee must frame all rules in Hindustani, with English serving only as a secondary translation. He argued passionately for the use of the national language. However, Dr. Sinha ruled him out of order, noting that his speech strayed into the broader topic of bilingualism rather than the procedural resolution.

Sovereignty and Authority
Historian Granville Austin noted that the Assembly’s power was embodied in these rules. A critical provision stated that the Assembly could not be dissolved except by a resolution supported by at least two-thirds of the total membership, ensuring the British could not dissolve the body except by force.

Adoption and Revision
Chairman Rajendra Prasad presented the report on December 20, 1946. After two days of discussion, the rules were adopted, though they were periodically refined until June 1949.
committees.title: Committee on the Rules of Procedure

committees.details:
Overview: Dedicated explicitly to defining the scope, meaning, and limitations of individual liberties that were to form the bedrock of Part III of the Constitution.

This highly consequential sub-committee took on the profound, philosophically dense task of sifting through dozens of international and domestic rights proposals to construct what would become the formidable Part III of the Constitution. Every individual right—ranging from the absolute abolition of untouchability, freedom of speech, and religious worship, to labor rights and equality before the law—was intensely scrutinized here.

The debates were remarkably rigorous, often pitting deep-rooted traditional conservatism against sweeping reformist ideals. The members engaged thoroughly on how to construct safeguards ensuring the government could maintain public order without reverting to colonial-era authoritarianism. This delicate balance resulted in the creation of 'reasonable restrictions' placed upon absolute liberties.

Perhaps their most significant structural contribution was splitting the proposed liberties into two monumental categories over multiple grueling sessions between February and April 1947. They defined 'justiciable rights' (freedoms that citizens could definitively enforce in a court of law against the State) versus 'non-justiciable rights' (aspirational social and economic targets). This clever categorisation eventually birthed the modern distinction between our enforceable Fundamental Rights and our guiding Directive Principles of State Policy.
committees.title: Sub-Committee on Fundamental Rights

committees.details:
Overview: Evaluated mechanisms for equitable political representation, cultural preservation, and targeted constitutional safeguards for diverse religious and linguistic minority groups.

Formed within the volatile crucible of escalating communal tensions pre and post-partition, the Sub-Committee on Minorities was tasked with an unimaginably burdensome mandate. They needed to draft permanent constitutional reassurances and protective legislation for India's wildly diverse religious and linguistic populations entirely without fostering permanent institutional divisions.

The most explosive and heavily debated subject was the future of 'separate electorates'—an extremely divisive system which the British colonial administration had previously employed to deepen communal divides. After agonizing discussions, the committee overwhelmingly concluded that fostering a united Indian identity demanded the total rejection of religion-based separate electorates.

However, realizing that marginalized groups still required guaranteed political safety nets, they engineered a powerful compromise mechanism. They recommended a comprehensive, historically significant system of politically reserved seats in legislative assemblies for specific underrepresented minority communities (like Scheduled Castes) for the initial developmental years of the Republic, ensuring representation without segregation.
committees.title: Sub-Committee on Minorities

committees.details:
Overview: Studied the unique geopolitical and cultural landscapes of Assam and surrounding tribal belts to create distinct administrative provisions, which evolved into Schedule VI.

Recognizing that the North-East Frontier and Assam's sprawling tribal territories possessed entirely distinct historical, social, and radically unique cultural structures structurally unlike any other part of the emerging nation, the Assembly empowered this highly specialized committee to investigate and build localized models of governance from the ground up.

The committee, led by Chief Minister Gopinath Bardoloi, travelled extensively through incredibly difficult terrain to consult locally with tribal chiefs and organizations. Their primary objective was to harmoniously integrate these sensitive geopolitical borderlands with democratic India seamlessly, without aggressively disrupting or imposing mainland administrative laws over deeply entrenched indigenous customs regarding land, forest, and social life.

Their findings and resulting groundbreaking recommendations laid the undisputed foundation for the visionary Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. They proposed the establishment of localized Autonomous District Councils (ADCs), a structural innovation allocating indigenous tribal communities the constitutional power to self-govern according to their own customary laws while remaining a proud, integral pillar of the Indian State.
committees.title: Committee on North East Frontier Tribal Areas

committees.details:
Overview: Examined the administrative setup, laws, and future governance models for centrally administered territories, acting as the precursors to modern-day Union Territories.

At the time of independence, distinct geographical and administrative areas such as Delhi, Ajmer-Merwara, Coorg, and the Andaman Islands were categorized under colonial law as Chief Commissioners’ Provinces. These territories were uniquely administered directly by the central government, almost entirely operating without democratic legislatures or self-governance. The fundamental question the Assembly faced was whether this centralized system should stubbornly continue in Independent India.

On July 30, 1947, Deshbandhu Gupta explicitly moved an amendment pushing for a dedicated research committee to formally determine the political future of these zones. Consequently, under Sitaramayya's chairmanship, the 7-member group held extensive meetings to review the administrative efficiency and demographic mechanics of the five prominent centrally controlled areas.

Instead of completely stripping their autonomy and mechanically merging them with geographically adjacent massive states, the committee recommended providing them with responsible, albeit functionally limited, local legislatures headed by a centrally appointed Lieutenant Governor. Rather than passing smoothly, these recommendations were fiercely debated in the Assembly but ultimately laid the structural groundwork detailing exactly how modern-day Union Territories are democratically administered today.
committees.title: Committee on Chief Commissioners’ Provinces
